content: The development of guidelines related to maternal and perinatal health involved a multidisciplinary group of experts, including consumer representatives. These experts brought diverse expertise in areas such as research, clinical practice, policy, program development, and gender equity. From this group, 16 external experts and stakeholders were invited to update the recommendations, focusing on the prevention and treatment of peripartum infections. The selection process emphasized diversity and expertise, ensuring no significant conflicts of interest. The GDG appraised evidence to inform the recommendations, particularly regarding the choice of antiseptic agents and methods for preoperative skin preparation for cesarean sections. The evidence was reviewed systematically, and the group reached unanimous consensus on the final recommendations. The GDG members are listed in Annex 1. An Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) was convened to conduct or update systematic reviews, appraise evidence, and develop evidence-to-decision (EtD) frameworks. A systematic review on the effects of antiseptic agents for preoperative skin preparation was updated, incorporating seven new studies involving 5,416 women. This review served as the primary source of evidence for the recommendations. The evidence was critically appraised using the GRADE methodology, and findings were summarized in GRADE tables. Representatives from the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group and methodologists attended GDG meetings to provide technical input and respond to queries. External partners and observers, including representatives from USAID, the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, participated in GDG meetings as observers. These organizations, with a history of collaboration with WHO, were identified as potential implementers of the recommendations. The list of observers is included in Annex 1. An External Review Group (ERG) of eight technical experts reviewed the final document to identify factual errors and provide feedback on clarity, contextual issues, and implementation implications. However, the ERG did not alter the recommendations formulated by the GDG. Members of the ERG are listed in Annex 1. Priority questions and outcomes for the recommendations were aligned with those from the 2015 WHO guidelines on maternal peripartum infections. Evidence was systematically searched, retrieved, synthesized, graded, and used to formulate the recommendations. The list of priority outcomes is provided in Annex 2. The evidence supporting the update was derived from multiple sources, including systematic reviews and data appraised using the GRADE approach. Certainty of evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as study design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Findings from qualitative reviews were appraised using the GRADE-CERQual tool, which assessed methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. The WHO Steering Group supervised the preparation of evidence summaries and EtD frameworks, which systematically considered evidence on effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The GDG reviewed these frameworks and reached consensus on the recommendations during a meeting held in October 2020. Recommendations were categorized as recommended, not recommended, context-specific, or research-context based on the evidence and judgment of the GDG. All GDG and ERG members were required to disclose potential conflicts of interest, which were reviewed and managed by the WHO Steering Group. Where conflicts were not significant, experts were required to declare them openly at the beginning of the GDG meeting. A summary of declarations and their management is provided in Annex 3. The GDG reviewed evidence summaries and deliberated on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, resource implications, acceptability, feasibility, and equity. Decisions were made by consensus, with no opposition from GDG members. Draft documents were prepared by the WHO Steering Group and reviewed by GDG and ERG members before finalization. External peer review was conducted by independent experts, and their feedback was incorporated to improve clarity and address factual errors. The guiding principles and best practices adopted by the GDG emphasized good clinical practice to improve care related to the prevention and treatment of peripartum infections. Protocols for managing maternal sepsis and septic shock were recommended, informed by international guidelines and adapted to local contexts. Efforts to reduce antimicrobial resistance were emphasized, with antibiotics recommended only when medically indicated. Hospitals were encouraged to establish committees to monitor antimicrobial usage and update formularies. These recommendations aim to optimize maternal and perinatal health outcomes while addressing equity, feasibility, and resource considerations.
